name: Methylphenidate
drug_class: Central nervous system stimulant; dopamine–noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor (piperidine)
route_note: Oral immediate-release tablets two to three times daily or once-daily extended-release (e.g. OROS) formulations; transdermal patch.

discovery.note: Synthesised in 1944; Panizzon named it Ritalin after his wife Marguerite ('Rita'), who reportedly used it to boost her tennis performance.

tagline: The most widely used ADHD stimulant, blocking dopamine and noradrenaline reuptake
summary: Methylphenidate is a CNS stimulant used for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder and narcolepsy. It blocks dopamine and noradrenaline reuptake and is available in many immediate- and extended-release formulations. It is a controlled substance because of its potential for misuse.
mechanism: Methylphenidate binds and blocks the dopamine and noradrenaline transporters, increasing extracellular levels of these neurotransmitters, notably in the prefrontal cortex and striatum. Unlike amphetamine, it does not cause substantial transporter-mediated release.
The d-threo enantiomer (dexmethylphenidate) accounts for most of the activity. Improved catecholamine signalling in prefrontal circuits is thought to enhance attention and impulse control in ADHD.
uses: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (children 6 and over, adolescents and adults)

history.title: Synthesis
history.detail: Leandro Panizzon synthesises methylphenidate at Ciba.

history.title: Launch
history.detail: Ciba introduces Ritalin as a mild stimulant.

history.title: FDA approval
history.detail: Methylphenidate is approved in the US.

history.title: Schedule II
history.detail: Methylphenidate is placed in Schedule II under the US Controlled Substances Act.

history.title: Concerta
history.detail: The OROS once-daily formulation is approved.

history.title: Daytrana patch
history.detail: The first transdermal ADHD medication is approved.

history.title: WHO EML
history.detail: Methylphenidate is added to the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines for ADHD.

history.title: Boxed warning update
history.detail: The FDA updates the stimulant boxed warning to emphasise abuse, misuse and addiction; supply shortages of ADHD stimulants persist.

pk.metabolism: De-esterification by carboxylesterase CES1 to inactive ritalinic acid

serious: Sudden death and serious cardiovascular events in people with heart disease
safety.boxed_warning: High potential for abuse and misuse, which can lead to substance use disorder, including addiction; misuse and abuse can result in overdose and death. Assess risk before prescribing and monitor throughout treatment.

facts: Methylphenidate is not metabolised by CYP enzymes but by carboxylesterase 1.
